en: Hung an elephant hide—
This was the Chinese custom.
It was three fathoms thick,
A hide entirely of elephant skin.
When it was time to beat it, a wrestler struck;
Its blow deafened the ears,
And its booming carried far.
The glory of great Beijing,
It raised its cast-iron head;
At command a wrestler struck it,
And lesser ears
Came away unable to hear.
The war drum was beaten hard;
Army upon myriad army massed,
Coming all together, none left behind.
There were peoples of many kinds;
The implacable Kalcha
Had warriors of many kinds prepared.
When he pondered, his words meant great turmoil;
His speech had no end.
Because of Tügöt's young hero,
He had reason to be troubled.
“Word has come from the khan;
What has mighty khan Kongurbai,
The great Kalcha, beheld?” they said.
Their iron-mesh armor,
Their gauntlets wholly of cast iron,
Their spears with peerless points,
Their swords with fearsome edges,
Their foot soldiers too heavy for horses,
Their giants of many kinds—
The wrestler with mighty arms,
Kazhby, who would strike the foe,
Broad-chested and stern-tempered,
The swaggering, proud-hearted one,
Had come without staying behind.
His warriors riding mules,
Who sped like beasts along the road,
His heroes accustomed to going on foot.
They dismounted on the open ground and shouted,
Calling out, asking where the enemy was;
His warriors had come,
When the Kalmyk sent word.
Of the Chinese clad in jackets,
Not one of the strongest stayed behind;
Of the Kalmyks clad in armor,
Not even their khans stayed behind.
They raised a tumult like a raiding host,
Struck their trumpets with a crash,
The drums boomed,
The brass pipes clattered,
They raised their dappled banners,
Asking, “Where is the foe we are to grapple?”
They raised a clamor for the khagan,
They were not few but many,
An army thronged through Beijing.
From the city of the khagan,
From the plains beyond it,
All those on this side stirred,
And around the gold-pillared pavilion
Forces of many kinds massed,
Not a few, but a multitude;
They had come crowding together,
Ready to serve the khan of the Kechil.
They had come prepared.
Some of them stood chafing,
The wrestlers were kept tethered;
If one should happen to break loose,
The man who tried to restrain him
Would have his shoulder torn out.
If he rushed in and struck with his fist,
Should the poor wretch be caught by it,
His life would leave him.
At the tower in Kendeme
They all came crowding together.
While his wrestlers stood like this,
He sent word and hurried them.
Algara, whom he rode to battle,
To tell how the battle had gone,
The accursed one made him prance,
Pacing him back and forth,
And hurried six thousand Chinese and countless kaldays,
Shouting aloud:
“Hear me, nobles; hear me, khan;
All my people here, listen!
He has girded his waist tight;
That orphaned slave who dwells in Beijing,
He seems to be a mighty hero,
And has pursued vengeance for his father Manas.
While we lay without posting scouts,
He unleashed havoc;
From the great racehorse Algara,
The offspring of that accursed one
He tore out the tail.
Algara has come back alive,
But he has become a sorry horse,
A stumpy black horse.
He has been disgraced.
Have you heard the news?
My black horse that I rode into combat
Had at his flanks
The wings of a mighty eagle.
The bloodthirsty man’s son tore out those wings.
When I look closely at Algara,
Forty calamities have struck him.
His dark haunches, which no whip could lash hard,
The haunches of Algara,
Have now been struck by a whip;
Unless he grows fat and recovers,
Disaster has overwhelmed him.
The blue coat upon me,
Its hem worn out and sleeves turned gray—
How can I wear it now?
Algara beneath me,
His bushy tail and beauty gone,
Looks about with his rump twitching—
With what face can I ride him?!
Today, my people, mark the date;
Eighty days from today,
Enter it in the register.
Take off your boots, stretch out your legs,
Grow fat and regain your strength!
When those eighty days have passed,
Then gather together,
Assemble without breaking ranks,
And obey this command.
Let not one of you remain behind;
Come to me, every one of you…”
Thus Kongurbay declared,
The great blue-gray-bearded Manchu,
The hulking swine.
He began his fury in earnest,
Saying, “This is the ruin awaiting whoever stays behind.”
Raging and snarling,
Roaring like a mountain boar,
He gave orders without cease.
He began a costly spectacle;
As for the people who had come,
And saying, “One who fails to come will see,”
See the tyranny of the Kalmyk—
He had them slaughtered.
He exalted his bloody rule above the people.
The tail of Algara
That hero-swine had fashioned
And ornamented with gold.
He had a tail stretched out in gold,
And to the craftsman who made it
He gave sixty fine young maidens,
Forty girls, to the craftsmen.
When the false tail was finished,
He had it fitted onto Algara.
Alooke’s Kongurbay,
Mounted Algara, whom no bullet could reach,
That playful thoroughbred steed;
He donned the blue coat no bullet pierced,
Such was the coat he chose to wear.
When Kongurbay grew enraged,
His hair bristled toward his face;
Such was the nature of the doomed one.
He fastened on his arms,
And pulled a deep-blue iron helmet
Down over his head.
His black hair, thick as a cudgel,
The infidel tied behind him
In two knotted sections.
Saying, “If I fight, I will be ready,”
He left none of his weapons behind;
The fortunate one put them on.
Double mail with lark-like rings,
Its collar distinct, its sleeves brass,
Made those it disliked curse;
Steel had been filed and worked into it,
And poured over every doubtful place.
No gun muzzle could bite it,
No spear point could penetrate it;
The mesh armor for his ribs—
The formidable Kalmyk donned
The iron that guarded his life.
Over the breadth of his shoulders
He again drew on iron.
The reason he equipped himself so
Was that when mighty Manas lived,
When Akkula and Algara
Pulled evenly, reins turned,
And they shouted from horseback,
Trading spear thrusts,
He had taken many a spear blow,
Collapsed and lost consciousness,
And despaired of his precious life.
Had the Kalmyk not seen it himself,
Back when his beard was blue-gray,
When he faced many young warriors?
Thinking, “I may suddenly die,”
The warrior Kalmyk pondered the disgrace.
He wound the gold-cheeked battle-axe
Around his wrist,
And the cast-iron mace with a head like a camel’s,
He took that along as well.
He was about to begin the upheaval;
Kongurbay had saddled
The swift horse Algara.
“Without taking the vast black army,
I will ride patrol and watch,
Skirting Mount Kaspan,
And divide the road into four.
They say he was born after his father,
The gray-maned Manas;
His figure and bearing,
His form astride a horse,
I will observe carefully and see.
Without seeing the young hero’s courage,
Why drive a host of ten thousand into turmoil,
Driving not a few but a multitude,
Driving them over forty days’ journey,
Driving them into a desert where they would perish,
Soring all the thoroughbred horses,
Paining the champions’ hearts,
Making some of them weep,
Making others ache,
Chilling the people’s spirits?
What inheritance would I gain?
If he is indeed a hero born of Manas,
I will meet him in the peopleless desert
And clash with him.
While my towering head still stands,
Why should I fear for nothing
A boy who has come without companions?
Without bringing ruin upon Beijing,
Without laying waste to my people,
I will get news from afar.
If he truly is Manas’s son,
I will reach him and put him to the test.
Without troubling my people,
I alone will go.
While my mighty head still stands,
How could I surrender my swift horse?
If Semetey is mighty,
I will clash with him and see.
While my strength is in its heroic prime,
How could I surrender my livestock?
The pale boy seems to have gone mad;
I will grapple with him and see!”
Thus Kongurbay declared.
He put on his blue coat,
Coiled like a blue tiger—
Such was Kongurbay’s nature.
His eyeglasses gleamed,
And a pendant-stone like a leather flask
Flashed on the crown
Of the Manchu doomed to burn and die.
From the palace with gates of steel,
The Kalmyk departed in turmoil,
Clad in armor no bullet pierced.
He slung the great six-grooved gun,
Ochogor, over his shoulder.
As though their Kalmyk would never return,
